analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA office dedicated to investigating and prosecuting anticompetitive practices by meatpackers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan support, never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up an Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside the Department of Agriculture, staffed with attorneys and armed with subpoena power, to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act — the century-old law governing meatpackers and livestock markets. It would also coordinate antitrust work with the Justice Department and FTC. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Cattle ranchers and poultry growers, who sell to a handful of dominant meatpackers and have long accused them of paying less than fair market prices; and consumers, who have faced rising meat prices that regulators link partly to limited competition in meat processing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ranchers, poultry growers, and grocery shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a dedicated office within USDA's Packers and Stockyards Division to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act, with authority to use subpoenas and bring civil or administrative actions under that law.

The office would serve as USDA's liaison to the Justice Department and FTC on competition and trade practices in the food and agricultural sector, and would consult with Homeland Security on food-supply security.

By putting specialized attorneys and investigators permanently on the enforcement job, the bill aims to give small ranchers and contract farmers a stronger counterweight against the large processors they sell to.

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies that would face dedicated investigations and lawsuits under the Packers and Stockyards Act, plus taxpayers who fund the new office.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new federal enforcement office on top of existing Justice Department and FTC antitrust authority, and critics of this approach argue duplication of enforcers has not historically broken up concentration in meat processing — the packers' share of the cattle market has grown even under existing law.

Litigation under the Packers and Stockyards Act is slow, and an office that can only bring civil and administrative actions under that one statute may not change processor behavior quickly; any costs of enforcement would ultimately be borne by taxpayers and possibly passed into food prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit is institutional: a permanent, specialized enforcement team aimed at a sector where a few companies buy the bulk of the nation's cattle and hogs. Its limits are real — it does not itself change any market rule or cap any price, it only strengthens the ability to sue, and enforcement under the Packers and Stockyards Act has historically been slow. It is a measured step, not a structural fix, and it died before anyone could test whether it would work.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its livestock subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Abigail Spanberger introduced the bill on June 23, 2021, joined by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican, making it a bipartisan introduction.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture, where it sat.
On July 28, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture — a step deeper into committee, not toward the floor.
No markup, vote, or further action is recorded; the bill's total action history is three entries, all referrals.
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican, in addition to the sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that dominate cattle and hog buying. They keep operating in a market where enforcement against anticompetitive practices remains scattered across agencies, and no dedicated USDA investigator exists to sue them. Ranchers and consumers are left with the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Abigail Spanberger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a USDA special investigator for meat and poultry competition.

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's one cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: President Biden
for.what_they_did: His July 2021 executive order on competition directed USDA to strengthen enforcement against meatpackers, aligning executive-branch pressure with the bill's goals.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Held the bill in committee without scheduling a markup
against.what_they_did: The committee took no recorded action beyond referring the bill to its Livestock and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee on July 28, 2021; it never came to a markup or vote before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor; it attracted little support in either party and died quietly in committee rather than along a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would point a permanent, subpoena-wielding prosecutor at the Packers and Stockyards Act — the main law governing how packers buy livestock and contract with poultry growers. The largest processors, which buy the great majority of the nation's cattle and hogs, would face the most exposure.

industries.industry: Cattle ranchers and contract poultry farmers
industries.note: These sellers deal with only a handful of buyers for their animals and birds, and a dedicated investigator would give them a stronger enforcement channel when they allege unfair pricing or contract terms. They would not pay for the office; taxpayers would.

Meat prices rose sharply in 2020-2021, and economists and regulators have pointed to thin competition in meat processing as a contributing factor. More enforcement could, over time, lower prices at the grocery counter, though the bill contains no direct price mechanism.
